blocks.x: The Manitoba rent increase guideline for 2027 is **3%**, effective January 1, 2027. At the same time, the province is raising the rent level at which units are exempt from rent regulation from $1,670 to $2,000 a month, which it calls the largest expansion of rent control in decades. More units will now fall under the guideline.
For property managers, that means capped increases on more units, and more reason to invest wisely in the ones you have.

On October 30, 2026, the province also cut how much capital work can count in an above-guideline application. The renovation solutions for property managers most likely to still make financial sense are the ones that cut costs or keep tenants.
The rules in brief
**Guideline:** 3% for increases taking effect in 2027.

**Exemption threshold:** rises to $2,000 a month on January 1, 2027. Most units renting below that amount are regulated. The exceptions include buildings first occupied after March 7, 2005, exempt for 20 years counted from the first occupancy permit or first tenant, whichever came first, along with social housing and government-run, co-op, non-profit life-lease and approved rehabilitated units.
**Notice:** tenants must receive written notice at least three months before an increase. For a January 1, 2027 increase, notice was due by September 30, 2026.
**Frequency:** rent generally can be raised only once every 12 months.

**Above-guideline increases:** landlords can apply to Manitoba's Residential Tenancies Branch for an increase above the guideline, based on documented changes in operating expenses and the allowable share of capital expenses. Mortgage interest is not an operating expense; it only counts if the complex runs at a deficit.

**New tenants:** a regulated unit in a complex of four or more units can't be rented to a new tenant above the average rent of similar units in the complex. In a complex of three units or fewer, the landlord sets the amount, and a fourplex with the landlord living in one unit counts as three.

**Notice to New Tenant:** for a regulated unit, the landlord must give this notice even if the rent isn't rising, and send the Branch a copy within 14 days. In a complex of four or more units, the tenant then has 30 days to ask the Branch to check the average. Without the notice, an increase isn't allowed.

**Moving a tenant out to renovate:** this applies only if the work needs the unit vacant. The landlord must give written notice to move. In Winnipeg that is currently 4 months, set from CMHC's fall vacancy rate, so it can change.

**Limits on that notice:** it can't end a fixed-term agreement early, and a tenant with a child at a nearby school can't be made to leave before the school year ends. The landlord pays reasonable moving expenses up to a set maximum. The tenant can ask in writing, before moving out, for first refusal on the renovated unit.

**Rehabilitation schemes:** with the Branch's approval, a scheme can cover a single unit for up to 2 years, or a complex or part of one for up to 5 years. Apply before you start, because the rules limit work done before the first order. For one unit in a complex of four or more, the tenant must leave voluntarily.
Renovations and above-guideline rent increases in Manitoba

If you've completed major capital work, such as a new roof, windows, boiler or building-wide upgrades, part of the cost may count in an above-guideline application. Landlords can't apply because they plan to do work. The Residential Tenancies Branch reviews the documented expenses and decides the allowable increase.

[On October 30, 2026](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/annual/2026/116.php), Manitoba cut the share of capital costs that counts in an above-guideline application by 40%. The share is now 20%, 15%, 10% or 7.5% of the cost, depending on the item. Since October 20, 2026, tenants pay none of a proposed above-guideline increase until the Branch issues an order.

The new shares apply to any application with no order by October 30, 2026, whenever it was filed. You can only claim costs already paid or billed, and you must list any rebates. The Branch's FAQ and fact sheet still show the old rule that tenants pay while they wait, but its home page notice replaces it.
To give yourself the best footing:
**Keep detailed records:** contracts, invoices, proof of payment, and before-and-after photos.
**Separate capital work from routine maintenance.** Repairs and upkeep are treated differently from capital improvements.

**Check the deadlines and forms** (Form 3 and the Branch's guidebook) before you start, not after. The Branch wants the application at least two and a half months before the first increase. Its landlord guide was last updated in September 2026, so it still shows the old shares and the old rule on paying before an order.
**Talk to residents.** Explain what's being upgraded and why. Clear communication reduces disputes.

If the building was built or renovated before 1990, check for asbestos before old materials are disturbed. Our guide covers [asbestos testing before you renovate](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).

If you're counting on an incentive, apply first. [Efficiency Manitoba's Building Envelope Program](https://efficiencymb.ca/business/building-envelope/) lists multi-unit residential buildings, and it says not to buy or install anything until you're approved.
Units above the $2,000 threshold

A unit is exempt if the rent payable on December 31 of the previous year was $2,000 or more. That is the regulation's wording. The Branch's FAQ says more than $2,000 a month as of December 31, 2026, so ask the Branch about a unit at exactly $2,000.
Starting in 2028, the amount rises each January by the guideline, rounded to the nearest $5.

Exempt units still follow the rules on three months' notice and one increase every 12 months, but the new-tenant limits don't apply to them. Well-finished, updated units in this range compete on quality, so renovations that keep them at the top of the market still matter.
The bottom line

With a 3% guideline, more units under rent control in 2027 and a smaller share of capital costs counting in an application, property managers win by spending on what lowers costs and keeps residents. Keep solid records of completed work in case an above-guideline application makes sense.
